# Study Tutorial: Learning-Assisted InSAR DEM Enhancement
## IEEE GRSS 2026 Data Fusion Contest — Complete Reference

> **How to use this document**: Read it top-to-bottom once to build mental models,
> then use section headers as a reference when working on specific modules.
> Each section answers: **What · Why · How · When · Principle · Method**.

---

## Table of Contents

1. [The Big Picture](#1-the-big-picture)
2. [Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) Fundamentals](#2-synthetic-aperture-radar-sar-fundamentals)
3. [Interferometric SAR (InSAR)](#3-interferometric-sar-insar)
4. [The Dataset: Capella Space X-band SAR](#4-the-dataset-capella-space-x-band-sar)
5. [Pair Graph & Temporal Baseline Strategy](#5-pair-graph--temporal-baseline-strategy)
6. [Classical InSAR Processing Pipeline](#6-classical-insar-processing-pipeline)
7. [Why Classical Methods Fail — The Problem We're Solving](#7-why-classical-methods-fail--the-problem-were-solving)
8. [Deep Learning Approach: Self-Supervised Denoising](#8-deep-learning-approach-self-supervised-denoising)
9. [The FiLM-Conditioned U-Net Architecture](#9-the-film-conditioned-u-net-architecture)
10. [Loss Functions & Physics Consistency](#10-loss-functions--physics-consistency)
11. [SBAS Time-Series Analysis](#11-sbas-time-series-analysis)
12. [Contest Metrics — What We're Optimizing](#12-contest-metrics--what-were-optimizing)
13. [The Complete Pipeline: End-to-End](#13-the-complete-pipeline-end-to-end)
14. [Code Architecture Map](#14-code-architecture-map)
15. [Key Equations Reference Sheet](#15-key-equations-reference-sheet)
16. [Glossary](#16-glossary)

---

## 1. The Big Picture

### What is this project?

We are building a **machine learning system that improves the quality of radar-derived elevation maps** (Digital Elevation Models, or DEMs) from satellite SAR data. The method is specifically designed for **InSAR** — Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar — a technique that measures surface height (and deformation) by comparing the phase of two radar images taken from slightly different positions.

### Why does it matter?

DEMs derived from InSAR are the primary way scientists measure:
- Volcanic ground deformation (Mauna Kea, Mauna Loa — our primary test site)
- Earthquake surface rupture
- Glacier dynamics and ice sheet melting
- Urban subsidence and infrastructure monitoring

Classical InSAR DEMs are noisy. Phase noise corrupts height estimates, and difficult terrain (dense vegetation, fast-moving lava, steep slopes) causes **decorrelation** — the radar signal loses coherence between two passes. Our DL system learns to denoise the interferograms before DEM extraction, improving all five contest quality metrics simultaneously.

### What is the contest asking for?

The IEEE GRSS 2026 Data Fusion Contest evaluates five metrics (explained fully in Section 12):
1. Triplet closure error ↓
2. Unwrap success rate ↑
3. Percent usable pairs ↑
4. DEM NMAD (Normalized Median Absolute Deviation) ↓
5. Temporal consistency residual ↓

Our system must demonstrate ≥30% improvement on metric 1, ≥15 pp on metric 2, etc.

### The key insight

Classical interferogram filters (Goldstein, BM3D) are **blind** — they don't know what satellite geometry produced the data. Our **FiLM-conditioned U-Net** is told the geometry (`Δt`, `Δθ_inc`, `B_perp`, orbit direction, look direction, SNR proxy), so it can adapt its denoising strategy per pair. This is the core scientific contribution.

---

## 2. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) Fundamentals

### What is SAR?

SAR is an **active microwave imaging radar** on a satellite. Unlike optical cameras that record reflected sunlight, SAR:
- Transmits its own microwave pulses (X-band = 9.6 GHz, λ ≈ 3.1 cm for Capella)
- Records the amplitude **and phase** of the returned echo
- Works day and night, through clouds
- Produces **complex-valued images** — each pixel has magnitude (backscatter) + phase

### The complex SLC

A **Single Look Complex (SLC)** image is the raw output:
```
pixel(r, a) = A(r, a) · exp(j·φ(r, a))
```
Where:
- `r` = range (distance from satellite to ground, measured by pulse travel time)
- `a` = azimuth (along-track position, synthesised by Doppler processing)
- `A` = amplitude (how strongly the ground reflects)
- `φ` = phase (fraction of wavelength in round-trip distance, wraps 0–2π)

### Why is phase useful?

The round-trip distance `2R` relates to phase as:
```
φ = -4π·R / λ      (for zero-squint)
```
A λ/2 = 1.55 cm change in slant range `R` causes a full 2π phase cycle. This extreme sensitivity is what makes InSAR capable of millimetre-scale deformation measurement.

### Capella spotlight mode

Capella satellites use **spotlight mode**: the antenna steers to dwell on one target area for an extended time. This gives:
- High azimuth resolution (~0.44 m) — better than stripmap
- Smaller scene extent (~5 km × 10 km per collect)
- Higher SNR per pixel
- **Trade-off**: smaller spatial coverage, so we need many collects to cover one AOI

### Speckle

SAR images are dominated by **speckle** — a multiplicative noise from coherent interference of many sub-resolution scatterers. It appears as a salt-and-pepper texture. Speckle makes single-pixel phase measurements unreliable. Solutions: multi-looking (spatial averaging), spectral filtering, or DL denoising (our approach).

---

## 3. Interferometric SAR (InSAR)

### What is InSAR?

InSAR forms an **interferogram** by multiplying two co-registered SLC images pixel by pixel:

```
φ_ij(p) = angle( SLC_i(p) × conj(SLC_j(p)) )
```

The resulting phase `φ_ij(p)` at pixel `p` contains:
```
φ_ij = φ_topo + φ_defo + φ_atm + φ_noise
```
- `φ_topo` — topographic contribution (from height difference + baseline)
- `φ_defo` — surface deformation between acquisitions
- `φ_atm` — atmospheric delay (water vapour, ionosphere)
- `φ_noise` — thermal noise + decorrelation noise

### Why the phase wraps

Phase is only measurable modulo 2π. A real interferogram looks like **fringes** — concentric bands where each band = one 2π cycle = one half-wavelength of range change. Phase unwrapping (Section 6.4) recovers the absolute phase from these wrapped measurements.

### Coherence: the quality indicator

**Coherence** γ measures how similar two SLC signals are at each pixel:
```
γ(p) = |<SLC_i · conj(SLC_j)>| / sqrt(<|SLC_i|²> × <|SLC_j|²>)
```
Range: 0 (fully decorrelated) to 1 (perfectly coherent).

Coherence is degraded by:
- **Temporal decorrelation** — vegetation growth, rain, lava flow changes the ground between passes
- **Geometric decorrelation** — large perpendicular baseline B_perp shifts the spectral overlap
- **Volume decorrelation** — radar penetrates into forest canopy, returns come from different depths
- **Thermal noise** — always present, inversely proportional to SNR

Coherence is critical: SNAPHU unwrapping fails in low-coherence regions (γ < 0.35).

### The perpendicular baseline B_perp

When two satellites observe the same point from slightly different positions:

```
          S1 ●                    ← satellite 1 position (ECEF)
              \
           B   \  ← baseline vector B = S2 - S1
              \
          S2 ●  \
                 \
                  ● T             ← target on ground

B_perp = component of B perpendicular to the look direction
B_par  = component of B along the look direction (range baseline)
```

**B_perp** determines:
1. **Topographic sensitivity**: `φ_topo = 4π·B_perp·h / (λ·R·sin(θ))` — larger B_perp → more phase per metre of height
2. **Geometric decorrelation**: critical baseline `B_crit = λ·R·sin(θ) / (2·δr_slant)` — if B_perp > B_crit → zero coherence

For Capella X-band spotlight: B_crit ≈ 39 km (very large). Our pairs have median B_perp = 6 m, max = 40 km, all well within the coherent range.

### Temporal baseline Δt

Longer temporal baseline = more deformation signal, but more temporal decorrelation. For Hawaii volcanic terrain (active lava, dense vegetation), coherence drops sharply after ~30–60 days. Our top pairs have Δt = 2.95 days (satellite revisit period), giving maximum coherence.

---

## 4. The Dataset: Capella Space X-band SAR

### Overview

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Satellite constellation | Capella-9 through Capella-14 |
| Center frequency | 9.6 GHz (X-band) |
| Wavelength λ | ~3.1 cm |
| Polarization | HH (horizontal transmit, horizontal receive) |
| Mode | Spotlight |
| Scene size | ~5 km × 10 km |
| Azimuth resolution | ~0.44 m |
| Range resolution | ~0.22 m |
| Format | COG GeoTIFF (CInt16 = complex int16) |
| Pixel spacing | 0.24 m (range) × 0.41 m (azimuth) |
| File size | 1.4–4.3 GB per SLC |

### Primary AOI: Hawaii (AOI_000)

```
Location: Big Island, Hawaii (19.4°N, 155.3°W)
Terrain: Active volcanic (Mauna Kea 4205m, Mauna Loa 4169m, Kīlauea active)
Collects: 221 SLCs
Orbits: 113 ascending + 108 descending
Pairs (loose): 8,834
Pairs (strict, 60d/2°): 3,033
Closure triplets: 24,171
Data volume: 497 GB
```

Why Hawaii is the best choice:
- Maximum number of collects → maximum pairs → strongest statistical metrics
- Both ascending + descending orbits → multi-geometry fusion possible (2.5D decomposition)
- High terrain relief → strong topographic signal → well-conditioned DEM NMAD metric
- Active vegetation + lava → high decorrelation baseline → large room for DL improvement
- Longest temporal span → richest SBAS time series

### STAC Metadata Structure

Each SLC has a companion `*_extended.json` sidecar with:
```
collect.state.state_vectors[]        ← ECEF position+velocity at 1s intervals (107 vectors)
collect.image.center_pixel.
    target_position                  ← ECEF ground target (metres)
    center_time                      ← nanosecond-precision UTC timestamp
    incidence_angle                  ← degrees
    look_angle                       ← degrees
collect.radar.center_frequency       ← 9.6e9 Hz
collect.image.pixel_spacing_row/col  ← metres
```

**Note**: Capella timestamps have nanosecond precision (`2025-04-21T13:14:17.274907138Z`).
Python 3.10 `fromisoformat()` only handles microseconds — must truncate to 6 decimal places.

---

## 5. Pair Graph & Temporal Baseline Strategy

### Why build a pair graph?

Not all combinations of SLC acquisitions make useful interferometric pairs. We need to:
1. Select only **compatible pairs** (same orbit direction, similar geometry)
2. Rank pairs by **quality** (short Δt, similar incidence = high coherence)
3. Find **triplets** for closure error computation
4. Build the **SBAS design matrix** A (time series inversion)

### Pair quality score Q_ij

```
Q_ij = 1 / (Δt_days + 1)  ×  1 / (1 + |Δθ_inc_deg|)
```

- `Δt_days`: temporal baseline in days. Short Δt → high temporal coherence.
- `Δθ_inc_deg`: incidence angle difference. Small Δθ → consistent geometry, better coregistration.

Constraints (hard filters applied before Q):
- `orbit_state` must match (both ascending OR both descending)
- `look_direction` must match (both left OR both right)
- Loose: Δt ≤ 365 days, Δθ ≤ 5°
- Strict: Δt ≤ 60 days, Δθ ≤ 2°

### Triplet closure and why it matters

A **triplet** (A, B, C) is a set of three acquisitions where all three pairs (A→B, B→C, A→C) exist.
The **triplet closure phase** is:
```
ε_closure = wrap( φ_AB + φ_BC − φ_AC )
```
In theory, for a noise-free, deformation-free stack: `ε_closure = 0`.
In practice, noise + atmospheric errors cause non-zero closure.

**Why use it?** Closure phase is a direct measure of phase noise that doesn't require a reference DEM.
Reducing median closure error is contest metric #1.

---

## 6. Classical InSAR Processing Pipeline

### Step 1: Coregistration

Two SLCs must be aligned to sub-pixel accuracy before forming an interferogram. Even a 0.1-pixel misalignment introduces significant phase error.

**Method** (our implementation in `scripts/preprocess_pairs.py`):
1. Intensity cross-correlation on a centre patch → integer pixel offset
2. Sub-pixel refinement via partial DFT upsampling (Guizar-Sicairos 2008, 10× precision)
3. Phase ramp shift via FFT: `shifted = IFFT( FFT(SLC) × exp(-2πi(dr·fr + dc·fc)) )`

### Step 2: Interferogram Formation

```python
ifg = SLC_ref × conj(SLC_sec)        # complex interferogram
```

The phase `angle(ifg)` at each pixel is the wrapped phase difference.

### Step 3: Multi-look (Coherence Estimation)

Average over a `looks_azimuth × looks_range` window:
```
γ(p) = |⟨ifg⟩_window| / sqrt(⟨|SLC_ref|²⟩ × ⟨|SLC_sec|²⟩)
```
More looks → better coherence estimate + smoother phase, but lower spatial resolution.
Typical: 5 × 5 looks (×25 effective averaging).

### Step 4: Goldstein Filtering

The Goldstein-Werner filter (1998) reduces phase noise in the spectral domain:

1. Divide interferogram into overlapping blocks (32×32 pixels)
2. For each block: compute 2D FFT → `spec = FFT2(ifg_block)`
3. Smooth spectral magnitude: `|S_smooth| = uniform_filter(|spec|, 3)`
4. Weight spectrum: `spec_filtered = spec × (|S_smooth|/max|S_smooth|)^α`
5. Inverse FFT → filtered block
6. Blend overlapping blocks with cosine taper

Parameter `α ∈ [0,1]`:
- `α = 0`: no filtering
- `α = 0.5`: moderate (standard)
- `α = 1.0`: maximum smoothing

**Adaptive variant**: `α(p) = α_max × (1 − γ(p))` — low coherence gets more filtering.

### Step 5: Phase Unwrapping (SNAPHU)

Wrapped phase is in `(−π, π]`. Phase unwrapping recovers the **absolute** phase by adding multiples of 2π:
```
Φ_unwrapped(p) = φ_wrapped(p) + 2π · n(p)
```
where `n(p)` is an integer determined by minimizing discontinuities.

**SNAPHU** (Statistical-cost, Network-flow Algorithm for Phase Unwrapping):
- Treats unwrapping as a minimum-cost network flow problem
- Uses coherence as per-pixel noise model
- Fails gracefully in low-coherence regions (marks them as "unconnected")

**Coherence mask**: pixels with γ < 0.35 are masked before unwrapping (they're too noisy to unwrap reliably).

### Step 6: Phase-to-Height Conversion

```
h(p) = Φ_unwrapped(p) × λ · R · sin(θ) / (4π · B_perp)
```
Where:
- `λ` = radar wavelength (0.031 m for X-band)
- `R` = slant range to target
- `θ` = incidence angle
- `B_perp` = perpendicular baseline

This gives **relative height** (DEM above a reference plane). Absolute DEM requires adding a reference elevation (e.g., SRTM or geoid model).

---

## 7. Why Classical Methods Fail — The Problem We're Solving

### The fundamental limitation

Classical filters like Goldstein operate **per-pair, blindly**. They don't know:
- How noisy the pair is expected to be (Δt = 3 days vs 100 days)
- What terrain type they're filtering
- What the pair geometry is (B_perp, incidence angle)
- Whether it's ascending or descending pass

The same filter is applied to a 3-day coherent pair over bare rock the same way as to a 60-day pair over tropical forest. This is suboptimal.

### The decorrelation problem visualized

```
Coherence vs. Temporal Baseline (Hawaii X-band, approximate):

γ
1.0 |●
0.8 |  ●
0.6 |      ●
0.4 |           ●
0.2 |                 ●          ●
0.0 |____________________________________ Δt (days)
    0    10    30    60   120   365
```

Below γ ≈ 0.35: SNAPHU fails to unwrap reliably.
The DL model's job: push the effective coherence threshold lower — make marginal pairs usable.

### Why deep learning is the right tool here

1. **Non-linear denoising**: DL can denoise complex phase patterns that linear filters cannot
2. **Geometry-awareness**: FiLM conditioning lets the model adapt to each pair's specific geometry
3. **Uncertainty quantification**: the model outputs per-pixel log-variance `log σ²(p)` → this feeds into uncertainty-weighted SBAS
4. **Self-supervised**: no clean reference interferograms exist. N2N training requires only pairs of noisy observations — which we create from sub-look splits of our SLCs

---

## 8. Deep Learning Approach: Self-Supervised Denoising

### The core challenge: no clean labels

In supervised learning, you train with `(noisy input, clean target)` pairs.
For InSAR, **no clean interferograms exist** — every real acquisition has speckle.

### Noise2Noise (Lehtinen et al. 2018)

The key insight: you can train a denoiser without clean data, as long as you can generate **two independent noisy observations of the same underlying signal**.

```
E[ f(x_noisy1) ] = E[ x_clean ]    ← standard supervised
E[ f(x_noisy1) ] = E[ x_noisy2 ]   ← Noise2Noise (equivalent if noise is zero-mean)
```

For InSAR: **sub-look splitting** creates two independent noisy versions of the same interferogram:

```
SLC acquisition
    ↓
Split bandwidth in frequency domain
    ↓
Sub-look 1 = lower-frequency half of spectrum → SLC_ref_1, SLC_sec_1
Sub-look 2 = upper-frequency half of spectrum → SLC_ref_2, SLC_sec_2
    ↓
ifg_A = SLC_ref_1 × conj(SLC_sec_1)   ← N2N input
ifg_B = SLC_ref_2 × conj(SLC_sec_2)   ← N2N target
```

Both `ifg_A` and `ifg_B` see the **same underlying phase** (same ground, same deformation), but with **independent speckle** (different frequency sub-bands → different resolution cells → uncorrelated noise). Phase correlation between sub-looks: **0.001** (measured on our data — essentially zero).

### Sub-look split: FFT method

```python
spec = FFT2(SLC)
spec = fftshift(spec)          # centre DC

# Sub-look 1: lower half of range bandwidth
sub_spec_1 = zeros_like(spec)
sub_spec_1[:, 0:N//2] = spec[:, 0:N//2]
SLC_sub1 = IFFT2(ifftshift(sub_spec_1)) * sqrt(2)   # amplitude correction

# Sub-look 2: upper half
sub_spec_2 = zeros_like(spec)
sub_spec_2[:, N//2:N] = spec[:, N//2:N]
SLC_sub2 = IFFT2(ifftshift(sub_spec_2)) * sqrt(2)
```

Trade-off: each sub-look has half the range bandwidth → √2 worse range resolution. This is acceptable — the denoised output from the full-bandwidth interferogram retains full resolution.

### Training data generation

```
For each SLC pair (ref, sec) in the top-100 by Q_ij:
    1. Read SLCs (windowed 1024×1024 patches from centre)
    2. Coregister sec to ref
    3. Split both SLCs into sub-looks (FFT method, range axis)
    4. Form ifg_A = sub_ref_1 × conj(sub_sec_1)
    5. Form ifg_B = sub_ref_2 × conj(sub_sec_2)
    6. Tile into 256×256 patches with 50% overlap
    7. Filter tiles with coherence_proxy < 0.2 (incoherent = no signal)
    8. Stack tile pairs (ifg_A, ifg_B) into training dataset
```

---

## 9. The FiLM-Conditioned U-Net Architecture

### Why U-Net?

U-Net is the standard architecture for dense prediction on images (same input/output spatial resolution). Its **skip connections** preserve fine spatial details (important for interferogram fringe patterns) while the encoder-decoder bottleneck learns high-level context.

```
Input: (B, 2, H, W)    ← Re(ifg) and Im(ifg) stacked as 2 channels
    ↓ encoder
    [64] → [128] → [256] → [512] → [1024]   ← feature maps per level
    ↓ bottleneck
    [1024]
    ↑ decoder (with skip connections)
    [512] → [256] → [128] → [64]
    ↓ output head
Output: (B, 3, H, W)   ← Re(ifg_clean), Im(ifg_clean), log_var
```

- Output channel 1+2: denoised complex interferogram
- Output channel 3: log-variance `log σ²(p)` — per-pixel uncertainty (used for SBAS weighting)

### What is FiLM conditioning?

**Feature-wise Linear Modulation** (Perez et al. 2018) injects external information into every layer of the network by **scaling and shifting** feature maps:

```python
# At each U-Net encoder/decoder block:
y_conditioned = γ(z) ⊙ y_features + β(z)

# where:
# y_features = standard conv output of shape (B, C, H, W)
# z = conditioning vector (geometry parameters)
# γ(z) = learned scale  (B, C, 1, 1)
# β(z) = learned shift  (B, C, 1, 1)
# ⊙ = element-wise multiplication (broadcast over H, W)
```

The conditioning network maps geometry vector → (γ, β) pairs for every feature map in every block.

### The geometry conditioning vector z

```python
z = [
    Δt_days / 365.0,          # normalised temporal baseline [0, 1]
    Δθ_inc_deg / 5.0,          # normalised incidence difference [0, 1]
    B_perp_m / 500.0,          # normalised perpendicular baseline [−1, 1]
    orbit_state,               # 0 = ascending, 1 = descending
    look_direction,            # 0 = left, 1 = right
    SNR_proxy,                 # mean(|SLC|²) / noise_floor estimate
]
# z ∈ R^6, all components in [−1, 1] after normalisation
```

### Why FiLM works for InSAR

- A 3-day ascending pair with B_perp = 50 m → low deformation phase, high temporal coherence → light denoising needed
- A 90-day descending pair with B_perp = 2 km → possible deformation + more decorrelation → heavier denoising needed
- Same U-Net backbone, but FiLM shifts its behaviour based on z → one model handles all geometries
- Zero-shot transfer: train on Hawaii, apply to LA without retraining — the geometry vector adapts automatically

### FiLM conditioning implementation sketch

```python
class FiLMBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, feat_channels, z_dim=6):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = ConvBnRelu(feat_channels, feat_channels)
        self.gamma_net = nn.Linear(z_dim, feat_channels)
        self.beta_net  = nn.Linear(z_dim, feat_channels)

    def forward(self, x, z):
        y = self.conv(x)                        # (B, C, H, W)
        γ = self.gamma_net(z)[:, :, None, None] # (B, C, 1, 1)
        β = self.beta_net(z)[:, :, None, None]  # (B, C, 1, 1)
        return γ * y + β                        # broadcast → (B, C, H, W)
```

---

## 10. Loss Functions & Physics Consistency

### L1: Noise2Noise Loss (self-supervised)

```
L_N2N = E[ ‖ f(ifg_A; z) − ifg_B ‖₁ ]
```

Train the network to predict sub-look B from sub-look A. Since both sub-looks converge to the same clean signal in expectation, the network learns to denoise. L1 (not L2) is used to avoid over-smoothing fringes.

### L2: Closure Consistency Loss

For every triplet (A, B, C) in the training batch:
```
L_closure = E[ ‖ wrap( φ̂_AB + φ̂_BC − φ̂_AC ) ‖₁ ]
```
Where `φ̂` is the predicted (denoised) phase. Pushes the network toward physically consistent phase estimates — denoised pairs must close in triplets.

This is the key loss that **directly minimises contest metric #1**.

### L3: Temporal Consistency Loss

Over a mini-stack of pairs sharing one common epoch:
```
L_temporal = E[ ‖ W(A·x − φ̂) ‖₂ ]
```
Where `A` is the SBAS design matrix (see Section 11), `x` is the estimated deformation time series, `φ̂` is the predicted phase, and `W = 1/σ²(p)` is the uncertainty weight. Forces consistency across the time series.

### L4: Gradient Smoothness Loss

```
L_grad = E[ ‖ ∇φ̂ ‖₁ ]    (total variation on denoised phase)
```
Prevents the network from producing high-frequency artefacts. Applied with a small weight.

### Total loss

```
L_total = w1·L_N2N + w2·L_closure + w3·L_temporal + w4·L_grad

Suggested weights: w1=1.0, w2=0.3, w3=0.1, w4=0.05
```

### Why uncertainty output?

The network outputs `log σ²(p)` — the log-variance of its prediction at each pixel.
Uses: `W(p) = 1/σ²(p)` as per-pixel weight in SBAS inversion (Section 11).
High uncertainty (low coherence regions, steep terrain) → down-weighted in the time series.
Low uncertainty (stable, coherent pixels) → up-weighted.

The uncertainty is trained implicitly through the N2N loss: pixels where sub-looks disagree more will have higher predicted uncertainty.

---

## 11. SBAS Time-Series Analysis

### What is SBAS?

**Small Baseline Subset (SBAS)** is a time-series InSAR method that uses a stack of many interferometric pairs to estimate the **surface deformation time series** at each pixel.

Given:
- `M` interferometric pairs
- `N` SAR acquisitions at times `t_1, ..., t_N`
- Each pair `(i, j)` → unwrapped phase `φ_ij`

SBAS solves:
```
A · x = φ̂     (system of M equations, N−1 unknowns)
```
Where:
- `A` is the M×(N−1) design matrix: `A[pair(i,j), k] = +1 if t_k in (t_i, t_j], else 0`
- `x` is the velocity vector (phase rate between consecutive epochs)
- `φ̂` is the stack of unwrapped interferometric phases

Solved via LSQR (least-squares with regularisation).

### Classical SBAS (baseline to beat)

```
min_x  ‖A·x − φ̂‖₂²    with uniform weights
```

### Uncertainty-weighted SBAS (our contribution)

```
min_x  ‖W(A·x − φ̂)‖₂²

where W(p) = diag(1/σ²_1(p), ..., 1/σ²_M(p))
```

`σ²_ij(p)` comes directly from our FiLMUNet's per-pixel log-variance output.
Pairs where the model is uncertain contribute less to the inversion.
This directly reduces the **temporal consistency residual** (contest metric #5).

### Multi-geometry fusion (Level 3)

With both ascending and descending orbits (Hawaii has both):
```
[A_asc  0   ] [v_E]   [φ̂_asc ]
[0    A_desc] [v_U] = [φ̂_desc]

→ 2.5D decomposition: East (v_E) + Vertical (v_U) displacement
```
Ascending sees predominantly East + Vertical; descending sees predominantly West + Vertical.
The joint inversion dramatically improves DEM NMAD (metric #4).

---

## 12. Contest Metrics — What We're Optimising

### Metric 1: Triplet Closure Error

```
median( |wrap(φ̂_AB + φ̂_BC − φ̂_AC)| )   over all triplets in the strict graph
```
**Target**: reduce by ≥30% vs classical Goldstein baseline.
**How we improve it**: `L_closure` loss forces the network to produce mutually consistent phases.

### Metric 2: Unwrap Success Rate

```
fraction of pixels successfully unwrapped (connected component ≥90% + closure gate)
```
**Target**: increase by ≥15 percentage points.
**How we improve it**: better denoised interferograms → higher effective coherence → more pixels above SNAPHU's threshold → larger connected components.

### Metric 3: Percent Usable Pairs

```
fraction of pairs where: coherence > 0.35 AND unwrap_pass AND closure_gate
```
**Target**: increase by ≥25 percentage points.
**How we improve it**: model denoises marginal pairs (γ ≈ 0.25–0.35) to make them usable.

### Metric 4: DEM NMAD

```
NMAD = 1.4826 × median( |e − median(e)| )    where e = DEM_predicted − DEM_reference
```
NMAD is a robust version of standard deviation (insensitive to outliers).
**Target**: reduce by ≥15%.
**How we improve it**: better phase quality → more reliable SNAPHU unwrapping → more accurate height conversion. Multi-geometry fusion (asc + desc joint inversion) adds large additional improvement.

### Metric 5: Temporal Consistency Residual

```
‖ W(A·x − φ̂) ‖₂    averaged over pixels and pairs
```
**Target**: reduce by ≥20%.
**How we improve it**: uncertainty-weighted SBAS `W(p) = 1/σ²(p)` down-weights noisy pairs, plus the L_temporal loss forces consistency during training.

### Summary Table

| Metric | Formula | Target | Our lever |
|--------|---------|--------|-----------|
| Triplet closure error | median\|wrap(φ_AB+φ_BC−φ_AC)\| | ↓ ≥30% | L_closure loss |
| Unwrap success rate | % pixels unwrapped | ↑ ≥15 pp | Better denoising → higher coherence |
| Usable pairs | % pairs passing QC | ↑ ≥25 pp | Marginal pairs denoised into usable range |
| DEM NMAD | 1.4826·median\|e−median(e)\| | ↓ ≥15% | Better unwrapping + multi-geom fusion |
| Temporal residual | ‖W(Ax−φ̂)‖₂ | ↓ ≥20% | Uncertainty-weighted SBAS |

---

## 13. The Complete Pipeline: End-to-End

```
Raw Capella SLC archives (AWS S3)
    │
    │ scripts/download_subset.py

data/raw/AOI_000/

Training tiles (N2N pairs):
```

# Study Tutorial: Learning-Assisted InSAR DEM Enhancement
## IEEE GRSS 2026 Data Fusion Contest — Complete Reference

> **How to use this document**: Read it top-to-bottom once to build mental models,
> then use section headers as a reference when working on specific modules.
> Each section answers: **What · Why · How · When · Principle · Method**.

---

5. [Pair Graph & Temporal Baseline Strategy](#5-pair-graph--temporal-baseline-strategy)

8. [Deep Learning Approach: Self-Supervised Denoising](#8-deep-learning-approach-self-supervised-denoising)
9. [The FiLM-Conditioned U-Net Architecture](#9-the-film-conditioned-u-net-architecture)
10. [Loss Functions & Physics Consistency](#10-loss-functions--physics-consistency)

---

## 1. The Big Picture

### What is this project?

We are building a **machine learning system that improves the quality of radar-derived elevation maps** (Digital Elevation Models, or DEMs) from satellite SAR data. The method is specifically designed for **InSAR** — Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar — a technique that measures surface height (and deformation) by comparing the phase of two radar images taken from slightly different positions.

### Why does it matter?

DEMs derived from InSAR are the primary way scientists measure:
- Volcanic ground deformation (Mauna Kea, Mauna Loa — our primary test site)
- Earthquake surface rupture
- Glacier dynamics and ice sheet melting
- Urban subsidence and infrastructure monitoring

Classical InSAR DEMs are noisy. Phase noise corrupts height estimates, and difficult terrain (dense vegetation, fast-moving lava, steep slopes) causes **decorrelation** — the radar signal loses coherence between two passes. Our DL system learns to denoise the interferograms before DEM extraction, improving all five contest quality metrics simultaneously.

### What is the contest asking for?

The IEEE GRSS 2026 Data Fusion Contest evaluates five metrics (explained fully in Section 12):

1. Triplet closure error ↓
2. Unwrap success rate ↑
3. Percent usable pairs ↑
4. DEM NMAD (Normalized Median Absolute Deviation) ↓
5. Temporal consistency residual ↓

Our system must demonstrate ≥30% improvement on metric 1, ≥15 pp on metric 2, etc.

### The key insight

Classical interferogram filters (Goldstein, BM3D) are **blind** — they don't know what satellite geometry produced the data. Our **FiLM-conditioned U-Net** is told the geometry (`Δt`, `Δθ_inc`, `B_perp`, orbit direction, look direction, SNR proxy), so it can adapt its denoising strategy per pair. This is the core scientific contribution.

---

## 2. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) Fundamentals

### What is SAR?

SAR is an **active microwave imaging radar** on a satellite. Unlike optical cameras that record reflected sunlight, SAR:
- Transmits its own microwave pulses (X-band = 9.6 GHz, λ ≈ 3.1 cm for Capella)
- Records the amplitude **and phase** of the returned echo
- Works day and night, through clouds
- Produces **complex-valued images** — each pixel has magnitude (backscatter) + phase

### The complex SLC

A **Single Look Complex (SLC)** image is the raw output:

```
pixel(r, a) = A(r, a) · exp(j·φ(r, a))
```

Where:
- `r` = range (distance from satellite to ground, measured by pulse travel time)
- `a` = azimuth (along-track position, synthesised by Doppler processing)
- `A` = amplitude (how strongly the ground reflects)
- `φ` = phase (fraction of wavelength in round-trip distance, wraps 0–2π)

### Why is phase useful?

The round-trip distance `2R` relates to phase as:

```
φ = -4π·R / λ      (for zero-squint)
```

A λ/2 = 1.55 cm change in slant range `R` causes a full 2π phase cycle. This extreme sensitivity
is what makes InSAR capable of millimetre-scale deformation measurement.

### Capella spotlight mode

Capella satellites use **spotlight mode**: the antenna steers to dwell on one target area for an
extended time. This gives:
- High azimuth resolution (~0.44 m) — better than stripmap
- Smaller scene extent (~5 km × 10 km per collect)
- Higher SNR per pixel

**Trade-off**: smaller spatial coverage, so we need many collects to cover one AOI.

### Speckle

SAR images are dominated by **speckle** — a multiplicative noise from coherent interference of
many sub-resolution scatterers. It appears as a salt-and-pepper texture. Speckle makes
single-pixel phase measurements unreliable. Solutions: multi-looking (spatial averaging),
spectral filtering, or DL denoising (our approach).

## 3. Interferometric SAR (InSAR)

### What is InSAR?

InSAR forms an **interferogram** by multiplying two co-registered SLC images pixel by pixel:

```
φ_ij(p) = angle( SLC_i(p) × conj(SLC_j(p)) )
```

The resulting phase `φ_ij(p)` at pixel `p` contains:

```
φ_ij = φ_topo + φ_defo + φ_atm + φ_noise
```

- `φ_topo`  — topographic contribution (from height difference + baseline)
- `φ_defo`  — surface deformation between acquisitions
- `φ_atm`   — atmospheric delay (water vapour, ionosphere)
- `φ_noise` — thermal noise + decorrelation noise

### Why the phase wraps

Phase is only measurable modulo 2π. A real interferogram looks like **fringes** — concentric bands
where each band = one 2π cycle = one half-wavelength of range change. Phase unwrapping (Section 6)
recovers the absolute phase from these wrapped measurements.

### Coherence: the quality indicator

**Coherence** γ measures how similar two SLC signals are at each pixel:

```
γ(p) = |<SLC_i · conj(SLC_j)>| / sqrt(<|SLC_i|²> × <|SLC_j|²>)
```

Range: 0 (fully decorrelated) to 1 (perfectly coherent).

Coherence is degraded by:
- **Temporal decorrelation** — vegetation growth, rain, lava flow changes between passes
- **Geometric decorrelation** — large perpendicular baseline B_perp shifts spectral overlap
- **Volume decorrelation** — radar penetrates forest canopy, returns from different depths
- **Thermal noise** — always present, inversely proportional to SNR

Coherence is critical: SNAPHU unwrapping fails in low-coherence regions (γ < 0.35).

### The perpendicular baseline B_perp

```
          S1 ●
              \
           B   \   ← baseline vector B = S2 - S1
                \
          S2     ●
                  \
                   ● T    ← target on ground

B_perp = component of B perpendicular to the look direction (in slant plane)
B_par  = component of B along the look direction (range baseline)
```

**B_perp** determines:

1. **Topographic sensitivity**: `φ_topo = 4π·B_perp·h / (λ·R·sin(θ))`
   Larger B_perp → more phase cycles per metre of height → better DEM precision, but also more
   geometric decorrelation.

2. **Critical baseline**: `B_crit = λ·R·sin(θ) / (2·δr_slant)`
   If B_perp > B_crit → zero coherence (complete geometric decorrelation).
   For Capella X-band spotlight: B_crit ≈ 39 km.
   Our pairs have median B_perp = 6 m, max = 40 km — all within the coherent range.

### Temporal baseline Δt

Longer Δt = more deformation signal, but more temporal decorrelation.
For Hawaii volcanic terrain (active lava, dense vegetation), coherence drops sharply after ~30–60 days.
Our top pairs have Δt = 2.95 days (satellite revisit), giving maximum coherence.

## 5. Pair Graph & Temporal Baseline Strategy

### Why build a pair graph?

Not all combinations of SLC acquisitions make useful interferometric pairs. We need to:
1. Select only **compatible pairs** (same orbit direction, similar geometry)
2. Rank pairs by **quality** (short Δt, similar incidence → high coherence)
3. Find **triplets** for closure error computation
4. Build the **SBAS design matrix** A for time-series inversion

### Pair quality score Q_ij

```
Q_ij = 1 / (Δt_days + 1)  ×  1 / (1 + |Δθ_inc_deg|)
```

- Short Δt → high temporal coherence → high Q
- Small Δθ → consistent geometry, better coregistration → high Q

**Hard constraints** (applied before Q):
- `orbit_state` must match (both ascending OR both descending)
- `look_direction` must match (both left OR both right)
- Loose: Δt ≤ 365 days, Δθ ≤ 5°
- Strict: Δt ≤ 60 days, Δθ ≤ 2°

**Results on Hawaii**: top pairs have Δt = 2.95 days, Δθ = 0°, Q = 0.253.

### Triplet closure and why it matters

A **triplet** (A, B, C) exists when pairs A→B, B→C, and A→C all exist.
The **closure phase** is:

```
ε_closure = wrap( φ_AB + φ_BC − φ_AC )
```

In theory (no noise, no deformation): `ε_closure = 0`.
In practice, noise + atmospheric path delay errors produce non-zero closure.

This is a noise metric that requires **no reference DEM** — making it ideal for self-evaluation.
Minimising median|ε_closure| is contest metric #1.

## 6. Classical InSAR Processing Pipeline

### Step 1: Coregistration

Two SLCs must be aligned to sub-pixel accuracy before interferogram formation.
Even 0.1-pixel misalignment introduces significant phase error.

**Our method** (`scripts/preprocess_pairs.py`):

```
1. Read 1024×1024 centre patches from both SLCs (rasterio windowed read)
2. Intensity cross-correlation via FFT → integer offset (r, c)
3. Sub-pixel refinement via partial DFT upsampling (±0.1 px precision)
4. Apply FFT phase ramp shift: IFFT( FFT(SLC_sec) × exp(-2πi(dr·fr + dc·fc)) )
```

Typical offsets on Hawaii pairs: dr ≈ 3–4 px (azimuth), dc ≈ 0.5–1 px (range).

### Step 2: Interferogram Formation

```python
ifg = SLC_ref × conj(SLC_sec_coregistered)   # complex, shape (H, W)
```

### Step 3: Coherence Estimation (Multi-look)

```
γ(p) = |mean_window(ifg)| / sqrt(mean_window(|SLC_ref|²) × mean_window(|SLC_sec|²))
```

Window: 5×5 looks (25 averaged samples). Result: coherence map [0, 1].

### Step 4: Goldstein Spectral Filter

**Why**: reduces phase noise while preserving fringe structure.

**How** (block-FFT approach):

```
For each 32×32 overlapping block of the interferogram:
    spec = FFT2(block)
    mag_smooth = uniform_filter(|spec|, 3)        // smooth spectral magnitude
    W = (mag_smooth / max(mag_smooth))^α          // weight by smoothed magnitude
    spec_filtered = spec × W
    filtered_block = IFFT2(spec_filtered)

Blend overlapping blocks with 2D Hanning window taper.
```

`α ∈ [0,1]`: 0 = no filter, 0.5 = standard, 1.0 = maximum.
**Adaptive variant**: `α(p) = α_max × (1 − γ(p))` — low coherence gets stronger filtering.

### Step 5: Phase Unwrapping (SNAPHU)

Wrapped phase `φ ∈ (−π, π]` → unwrapped phase `Φ = φ + 2π·n` where `n` is an integer field.

**SNAPHU** solves this as a minimum-cost network flow problem using coherence as the noise model.
Pixels with γ < 0.35 are masked (too noisy to unwrap reliably).

### Step 6: Phase-to-Height Conversion

```
h(p) = Φ(p) × λ · R · sin(θ) / (4π · B_perp)
```

This gives relative height. Adding a reference elevation (e.g., SRTM) yields an absolute DEM.

## 7. Why Classical Methods Fail — The Problem We're Solving

### The fundamental limitation of classical filters

Classical filters (Goldstein, BM3D) are **geometry-blind**:
- They don't know that a 3-day pair is inherently less noisy than a 60-day pair
- They don't adapt to terrain type, orbit geometry, or acquisition mode
- The same `α` parameter is applied to a coherent urban pair and a decorrelated lava pair

### The decorrelation problem

```
Coherence vs. Temporal Baseline (Hawaii X-band, approximate):

γ  1.0 |●
   0.8 |  ●
   0.6 |     ●
   0.4 |          ●
   0.2 |                ●           ●
   0.0 |___________________________________  Δt (days)
         0   10   30   60   120   365
         ↑                 ↑
      Best pairs      Already unusable
                      without DL denoising
```

Below γ ≈ 0.35: SNAPHU fails reliably. These pairs are currently discarded.
The DL model's job: push the effective usable coherence threshold from 0.35 down to ~0.20.

### Why deep learning is the right tool

| Property | Classical Goldstein | FiLM U-Net |
|----------|--------------------|-----------:|
| Geometry-aware | No | Yes (FiLM conditioning) |
| Adaptive to coherence | Partially (adaptive-α) | Yes (trained end-to-end) |
| Uncertainty estimate | No | Yes (log-variance output) |
| Preserves fringes | Partially | Better (trained on fringes) |
| Transfer to new AOI | No (must retune) | Yes (zero-shot via z vector) |
| Requires clean labels | N/A | No (N2N self-supervised) |

## 8. Deep Learning Approach: Self-Supervised Denoising

### The core challenge: no clean labels

In supervised learning: train with `(noisy_input, clean_target)` pairs.
For InSAR: **no clean interferograms exist** — every real acquisition has speckle.

### Noise2Noise principle

Key theorem (Lehtinen et al. 2018):

> If you train a network to predict `x_noisy2` from `x_noisy1`, and both observations have
> zero-mean independent noise on top of the same underlying signal `x_clean`, then the trained
> network will converge to predicting `x_clean`.

```
Standard:   E[ f(x_noisy) ] → x_clean     (requires clean labels)
N2N:        E[ f(x_noisy1) ] → E[ x_noisy2 ] = x_clean  (requires two noisy obs.)
```

For InSAR: **sub-look splitting** creates two independent noisy observations.

### Sub-look splitting: the mechanism

A Capella SLC uses a ~600 MHz range bandwidth. Splitting at the midpoint:

```
Full-bandwidth SLC  →  FFT along range  →  fftshift (DC at centre)
                                               ↓
                        Lower half: freq 0 to N/2  → Sub-look 1
                        Upper half: freq N/2 to N  → Sub-look 2
                                               ↓
                        Both → IFFT → sub-look SLCs (half bandwidth each)
```

Sub-look 1 and Sub-look 2:
- See the **same ground** (same geometry, same deformation, same topography)
- Have **independent speckle** (different resolution cells from different frequency bands)
- Measured phase cross-correlation on our Hawaii data: **0.001** ≈ fully independent

Therefore:
```
ifg_A = sub_ref_1 × conj(sub_sec_1)   ← N2N input
ifg_B = sub_ref_2 × conj(sub_sec_2)   ← N2N target
```

Training: minimise `E[‖ FiLMUNet(ifg_A, z) − ifg_B ‖₁]`

### Training data generation summary

```
For each of the top-100 Hawaii pairs (by Q_ij):
  1. Read 1024×1024 patches from centre of both SLCs
  2. Coregister (cross-correlation + sub-pixel shift)
  3. Split each SLC into sub-look 1 and sub-look 2 (FFT, range axis)
  4. Form ifg_A and ifg_B
  5. Extract 256×256 tiles with 50% overlap → ~49 tiles per pair
  6. Skip tiles with coherence_proxy < 0.2 (no signal)
  7. Compute z vector: [Δt/365, Δθ/5, B_perp/500, orbit, look, SNR_proxy]
```

Total training examples: ~100 pairs × ~30 valid tiles = ~3,000 tile pairs.

## 9. The FiLM-Conditioned U-Net Architecture

### Why U-Net?

U-Net (Ronneberger et al. 2015) is the standard for dense prediction tasks:
- **Skip connections**: preserve fine spatial detail (fringe patterns, edges)
- **Encoder-decoder**: bottleneck learns context; decoder restores resolution
- Works well on complex-valued data when split into real+imaginary channels

### Model I/O

```
Input :  (B, 2, H, W)   — channel 0: Re(ifg_A), channel 1: Im(ifg_A)
                          + geometry vector z ∈ R^6

Output:  (B, 3, H, W)   — channels 0,1: Re(ifg_clean), Im(ifg_clean)
                          — channel 2: log_var(p) = log σ²(p)  (uncertainty)
```

### FiLM conditioning

At **every encoder and decoder block**, the feature maps are modulated by the geometry:

```
y_conditioned = γ(z) ⊙ y_features + β(z)

where:
  y_features  shape (B, C, H, W)   — output of standard conv-BN-ReLU
  γ(z)        shape (B, C, 1, 1)   — per-channel scale  (broadcast over H, W)
  β(z)        shape (B, C, 1, 1)   — per-channel shift
  z           shape (B, 6)          — geometry conditioning vector
```

The conditioning network: `MLP(z) → [γ_1, β_1, γ_2, β_2, ..., γ_L, β_L]`
where L = number of FiLM blocks (one per encoder/decoder level).

### The geometry conditioning vector z

```python
z = [
    Δt_days / 365.0,          # [0, 1]
    Δθ_inc_deg / 5.0,          # [0, 1]
    B_perp_m / 500.0,          # [-1, 1] (signed, positive = sec farther)
    float(orbit == 'ascending'),  # {0, 1}
    float(look == 'right'),       # {0, 1}
    SNR_proxy,                 # mean(|SLC|²) / noise_floor estimate, normalised
]
```

### Network architecture (encoder levels)

```
Level 0:  2ch  → 64ch   FiLM-block + pool
Level 1: 64ch  → 128ch  FiLM-block + pool
Level 2: 128ch → 256ch  FiLM-block + pool
Level 3: 256ch → 512ch  FiLM-block + pool
Bottleneck: 512ch → 1024ch FiLM-block

Level 3: 1024+512 → 512ch FiLM-block + upsample
Level 2:  512+256 → 256ch FiLM-block + upsample
Level 1:  256+128 → 128ch FiLM-block + upsample
Level 0:  128+64  →  64ch FiLM-block + upsample

Output:  64ch → 3ch  (1×1 conv, no activation on log_var)
```

## 10. Loss Functions & Physics Consistency

### L1 — Noise2Noise (self-supervised, primary)

```
L_N2N = mean( | f(ifg_A; z) − ifg_B | )     [complex L1, or split Re/Im]
```

Trains the network to predict one sub-look interferogram from the other.
L1 (not L2) preserves sharp fringe transitions.

### L2 — Closure Consistency

```
L_closure = mean( | wrap( φ̂_AB + φ̂_BC − φ̂_AC ) | )     over all triplets in batch
```

Where `φ̂` is the predicted (denoised) phase. Directly minimises contest metric #1.
A network trained only with L_N2N may not produce closure-consistent phases —
L_closure is necessary for the triplet metric.

### L3 — Temporal Consistency

```
L_temporal = mean( || W · (A · x − φ̂) ||₂ )     over mini-stacks

where:
  A  = SBAS design matrix (mini-batch of connected pairs)
  x  = estimated velocity from LSQR(A, φ̂)
  φ̂ = model's predicted phases
  W  = 1/σ²(p)  from model's log_var output
```

Forces model predictions to be consistent with the SBAS time-series. Directly reduces metric #5.

### L4 — Gradient Smoothness (regulariser)

```
L_grad = mean( |∂φ̂/∂x| + |∂φ̂/∂y| )     [total variation]
```

Prevents high-frequency artefacts in denoised output. Small weight only.

### Combined loss

```
L = 1.0 · L_N2N  +  0.3 · L_closure  +  0.1 · L_temporal  +  0.05 · L_grad
```

### The uncertainty output log σ²(p)

The network outputs `log σ²(p)` at every pixel. Two uses:

1. **During training**: log-likelihood loss term — pixels where model is uncertain contribute less.
2. **At inference**: `W(p) = 1/σ²(p) = exp(-log_var(p))` feeds into uncertainty-weighted SBAS.

---

## 11. SBAS Time-Series Analysis

### What is SBAS?

**Small Baseline Subset** estimates a **surface deformation time series** from many interferometric
pairs. Given `N` SAR acquisitions and `M` pairs, it solves the linear system:

```
A · x = φ̂

A ∈ R^{M × (N-1)}    — design matrix: A[pair(i,j), k] = +1 if t_k ∈ (t_i, t_j], else 0
x ∈ R^{N-1}           — phase velocity between consecutive epochs
φ̂ ∈ R^M              — observed unwrapped phases
```

Solved via least-squares (LSQR with Tikhonov regularisation for underdetermined systems).

### Classical SBAS (baseline)

```
min_x  || A·x − φ̂ ||₂²    (uniform weights)
```

### Uncertainty-weighted SBAS (our key contribution)

```
min_x  || W · (A·x − φ̂) ||₂²

W = diag(1/σ²_1, ..., 1/σ²_M)    ← from FiLMUNet log-variance output
```

Pairs where the model is uncertain → small weights → contribute less to inversion.
Result: more robust time series, lower temporal residual (metric #5).

### Multi-geometry fusion (ascending + descending)

With both orbit geometries (Hawaii has 113 asc + 108 desc):

```
[A_asc    0    ] [ v_E ]   [ φ̂_asc  ]
[  0    A_desc ] [ v_U ] = [ φ̂_desc ]

→ joint inversion gives East (v_E) and Vertical (v_U) displacement components
```

Ascending radar LOS is ~east-looking; descending is ~west-looking.
Combined: separates E/W horizontal from vertical deformation.
Dramatically improves DEM NMAD (metric #4).

## 12. Contest Metrics — What We're Optimising

### Metric 1: Triplet Closure Error

```
score = median( |wrap(φ̂_AB + φ̂_BC − φ̂_AC)| )    over all triplets
```

Target: ↓ ≥30% vs classical Goldstein.
Our lever: **L_closure loss** during FiLMUNet training.
Measurement: 24,171 strict triplets over Hawaii.

### Metric 2: Unwrap Success Rate

```
score = fraction of pixels in successfully unwrapped connected component (≥90% coverage + closure gate)
```

Target: ↑ ≥15 percentage points.
Our lever: better denoised interferograms → higher effective coherence → SNAPHU unwraps more pixels.

### Metric 3: Percent Usable Pairs

```
score = fraction of pairs where: γ > 0.35  AND  unwrap_pass  AND  closure_gate
```

Target: ↑ ≥25 percentage points.
Our lever: model denoises marginal pairs (γ ≈ 0.20–0.35) to cross the usability threshold.

### Metric 4: DEM NMAD

```
NMAD = 1.4826 × median( |e − median(e)| )    where e = DEM_our − DEM_reference
```

NMAD is a robust standard deviation (1.4826 scales median absolute deviation to match σ for Gaussian).
It is insensitive to outliers (cliffs, water bodies, layover), unlike RMSE.

Target: ↓ ≥15%.
Our lever: better phase + multi-geometry 2.5D fusion.

### Metric 5: Temporal Consistency Residual

```
score = || W(A·x − φ̂) ||₂    averaged over pixels and pairs
```

Target: ↓ ≥20%.
Our lever: uncertainty-weighted SBAS + L_temporal training loss.

### Summary

| # | Metric | Formula | Target | Primary lever |
|---|--------|---------|--------|---------------|
| 1 | Triplet closure | median\|wrap(φ_AB+φ_BC−φ_AC)\| | ↓ ≥30% | L_closure loss |
| 2 | Unwrap success | % pixels unwrapped | ↑ ≥15 pp | Better denoising |
| 3 | Usable pairs | % pairs passing QC | ↑ ≥25 pp | Marginal pairs recovered |
| 4 | DEM NMAD | 1.4826·median\|e−median(e)\| | ↓ ≥15% | Better unwrapping + multi-geom |
| 5 | Temporal residual | \|\|W(Ax−φ̂)\|\|₂ | ↓ ≥20% | Uncertainty-weighted SBAS |

| Phase-to-height | `h = Φ·λ·R·sin θ / (4π·B_perp)` | metres |
| Critical baseline | `B_crit = λ·R·sin θ / (2·δr_slant)` | metres (~39 km Capella) |
| Q_ij score | `Q = 1/(Δt+1) × 1/(1+\|Δθ\|)` | (0, 1] |
| Closure phase | `ε = wrap(φ_AB + φ_BC − φ_AC)` | radians |
| DEM NMAD | `1.4826 × median(\|e − median(e)\|)` | metres |
| SBAS system | `A·x = φ̂` | radians |
| Weighted SBAS | `min_x ‖W(Ax−φ̂)‖₂ , W=1/σ²` | — |
| FiLM modulation | `y' = γ(z)⊙y + β(z)` | — |
| N2N loss | `E[‖f(ifg_A; z) − ifg_B‖₁]` | radians |
| Closure loss | `E[\|wrap(φ̂_AB + φ̂_BC − φ̂_AC)\|₁]` | radians |
| Temporal loss | `E[‖W(Ax−φ̂)‖₂]` | — |
| Total loss | `L_N2N + 0.3·L_closure + 0.1·L_temporal + 0.05·L_grad` | — |

---

## 16. Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|-----------|
| **SLC** | Single Look Complex — focused SAR image storing amplitude + phase per pixel |
| **DEM** | Digital Elevation Model — raster of surface height (metres above reference) |
| **InSAR** | Interferometric SAR — measures height/deformation from phase difference of 2 SLCs |
| **Interferogram** | `SLC_i × conj(SLC_j)` — phase encodes topography + deformation |
| **Coherence γ** | Signal similarity [0,1] between two SLCs; below ~0.35 phase is unreliable |
| **Phase unwrapping** | Recovering absolute phase from wrapped (−π, π] measurements |
| **SNAPHU** | Leading phase unwrapping algorithm using minimum-cost network flow |
| **B_perp** | Perpendicular baseline — satellite offset perpendicular to the look direction |
| **B_crit** | Critical baseline — B_perp beyond which geometric decorrelation is complete |
| **Δt** | Temporal baseline — time (days) between two SAR acquisitions |
| **SBAS** | Small Baseline Subset — multi-pair time-series InSAR method |
| **Speckle** | Multiplicative noise in SAR from coherent interference of sub-pixel scatterers |
| **Multi-look** | Spatial averaging to reduce speckle (trades resolution for SNR) |
| **Goldstein filter** | FFT-domain interferogram filter weighting spectrum by \|S\|^α |
| **FiLM** | Feature-wise Linear Modulation — conditioning CNN features on external vector z |
| **U-Net** | Encoder-decoder CNN with skip connections; standard for dense prediction |
| **N2N** | Noise2Noise — self-supervised denoising using two independent noisy observations |
| **Sub-look** | Spectral subset of SLC (half bandwidth) — provides independent speckle realisation |
| **Triplet** | Three acquisitions A, B, C where all three pairwise interferograms exist |
| **Closure error** | Non-zero `wrap(φ_AB + φ_BC − φ_AC)` — measure of phase noise or unwrapping error |
| **AOI** | Area of Interest — geographic cluster of SAR acquisitions (39 in the contest) |
| **COG** | Cloud-Optimised GeoTIFF — HTTP range-request-friendly raster format |
| **CInt16** | Complex 16-bit integer — Capella's compact SLC storage format |
| **ECEF** | Earth-Centred Earth-Fixed Cartesian coordinates (metres from Earth's centre) |
| **Q_ij** | Pair quality score combining temporal and geometric quality terms |
| **NMAD** | Normalised Median Absolute Deviation — robust scatter metric, outlier-insensitive |
| **2.5D** | East + Vertical displacement from joint ascending + descending inversion |
| **Zero-shot transfer** | Applying a trained model to a new AOI without any retraining |
| **log_var** | Per-pixel log-variance output — the model's uncertainty estimate |
| **SNR_proxy** | Estimated signal-to-noise ratio from SLC amplitude statistics |
